title: How Owls Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore owls: their global range and roughly 250 species, the two families (barn owls, Tytonidae, and true owls, Strigidae), big front-facing eyes and night vision, ear tufts and asymmetrical ears, facial disc hearing, head rotation and the blood-pooling mechanism, silent flight through serrated and fringed feathers, hunting methods (perch and pounce, quartering, helicoptering), digestion and owl pellets, roosting and nesting (including owls in saguaro cacti and stolen burrows), communal roosts, mating calls and sky dances, owlet development and what to do with fledglings on the ground, owl folklore from Athena to Julius Caesar, owl cafes in Japan, and a listener mail correction on condom effectiveness.

segments.title: Opening banter and owl sounds
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck share anecdotes about owls seen and heard near their homes and discuss owl calls, including the Eastern screech owl's whinny.

segments.title: Owl anatomy, eyes and night vision
segments.summary: The hosts describe owls' large, round, front-facing eyes, binocular vision, night vision, the black eyes of strictly nocturnal species, and their broad wingspan and short tails. Owls have existed for about 55 million years and live on every continent except Antarctica, with about 250 species.

segments.title: Ear tufts, hearing and facial discs
segments.summary: Ear tufts are feathers that do not aid hearing and may be used to communicate. Owls have asymmetrical ears that help pinpoint prey hidden under snow or leaves, and their facial feather discs funnel sound like a satellite dish.

segments.title: Barn owls versus true owls
segments.summary: Owls are split into two families: barn owls (Tytonidae, about 17 species, heart-shaped face, hissing call) and true owls (Strigidae, the rest, rounded disc face). The hosts compare the barred owl's hoot to 'who cooks for y'all' and describe the elf owl and other species.

segments.title: Owl head rotation and blood circulation
segments.summary: Owls cannot move their eyeballs, so they turn their heads roughly 270 degrees. A pooling mechanism for blood keeps the eyes and brain supplied when circulation is cut off at extreme rotation.

segments.title: Owl habitat, roosting and nesting
segments.summary: Owls need food, a roost, and a nest. They are known for stealing nests and burrows. Owls live in deserts, nesting in saguaro cacti, and in many habitats including suburbs, and burrowing owls use abandoned burrows. Owls also run on the ground, and barn owl chicks stand upright.

segments.title: Silent flight
segments.summary: Owls fly nearly silently due to broad wings, serrated leading wing edges that break up turbulence, soft fringed feathers that dampen sound, and sound shifted to frequencies prey cannot hear.

segments.title: Owl diet, digestion and pellets
segments.summary: Owls use talons to catch prey and their beaks to kill it, then swallow prey whole when possible. Indigestible parts stay in the gizzard for up to ten hours and are regurgitated as pellets. Owls also hunt by perch-and-pounce, quartering flight, and helicoptering, and they sometimes share communal roosts and are mobbed by smaller birds.

segments.title: Owl mating, eggs and owlets
segments.summary: Males call to attract females and perform sky dances. Females lay several eggs, incubate for about 24 to 32 days, and lose belly feathers to warm the eggs. Owlets are helpless until they can thermoregulate, then branch out or sit on the ground, where people should leave them alone.
